stem: Which broader change in western mining does Twain's description of Virginia City best illustrate?

stimulus.source_note: Mark Twain, Roughing It (1872), ch. 52. Public domain. Text verified against the Standard Ebooks edition (standardebooks.org/ebooks/mark-twain/roughing-it/text/chapter-52).
stimulus.text:
Mark Twain, Roughing It (1872), Chapter 52, on Virginia City, Nevada:

"The year 1863 was perhaps the very top blossom and culmination of the 'flush times.' Virginia swarmed with men and vehicles to that degree that the place looked like a very hive—that is when one's vision could pierce through the thick fog of alkali dust that was generally blowing in summer... Speculation ran riot, and yet there was a world of substantial business going on, too. All freights were brought over the mountains from California (150 miles) by pack-train partly, and partly in huge wagons drawn by such long mule teams that each team amounted to a procession... All the bullion was shipped in bars by stage to San Francisco... There were three stages a day, each way, and I have seen the out-going stages carry away a third of a ton of bullion each, and more than once I saw them divide a two-ton lot and take it off."

"All along under the center of Virginia and Gold Hill, for a couple of miles, ran the great Comstock silver lode — a vein of ore from fifty to eighty feet thick between its solid walls of rock — a vein as wide as some of New York's streets."

"Virginia was a busy city of streets and houses above ground. Under it was another busy city, down in the bowels of the earth, where a great population of men thronged in and out among an intricate maze of tunnels and drifts, flitting hither and thither under a winking sparkle of lights, and over their heads towered a vast web of interlocking timbers that held the walls of the gutted Comstock apart."

options.text: Mining stayed a business of lone prospectors with pans and shovels
options.misconception: Background: Twain's underground city of tunnels and timbering needed capital no lone prospector had; placer mining was the early stage, not the lasting one.

options.text: Mining moved west to east as the gold in California ran out
options.misconception: Background: mining spread across the West, but the change Twain shows is in how mining was organized, not in which direction it moved.

options.text: Mining was outlawed in Nevada after the Comstock Lode was found
options.misconception: Background: Nevada mining was never outlawed; the Comstock mines operated for decades and made Virginia City one of the West's largest towns.

options.text: Mining became an industrial business run by large companies with wage workers

rationales.A: Background from the books: placer mining with pans and sluices came first, but the deep lode needed expensive machinery — hoists, pumps, and stamp mills, so large firms took over and wage workers replaced prospectors.
rationales.B: Background: the mines did spread from California to Nevada and beyond, but Twain's passage shows a change in scale and organization, not geography.
rationales.C: Background: the Comstock mines ran for decades under private ownership. No ban followed the strike; the strike is what built the town.
rationales.D: Twain's underground city proves it: miles of tunnels, a web of timbers, whole crews working shifts. That is a factory below ground, run by companies, not a prospector's camp.
rationales.general:
Think of the mine as a factory that happens to sit underground.
1. Measure the scale Twain shows: miles of tunnels, a vast web of timbers, crowds of men working below.
2. Ask who could pay for that. Background: no lone prospector could; only a company with capital and wage workers could.
3. Name the change. Background: mining grew up from panning to industry, with investors, shares, and hired hands.
Remember: when the tool gets too big for one person, the business stops being one person's.
